records.name: Denominators and conditional probability
records.tldr: A percentage answers a question about a particular group. Name that group before interpreting the number, and keep unknown outcomes separate from measured non-response.
records.summary: A proportion identifies an outcome within a defined group. The denominator might be everyone enrolled, everyone treated, people with an evaluable scan, or only people with a recurrence; those answer different questions. Conditional probability makes the specified group explicit and is not a statement of causation. Repeated measurements do not create new independent people. Unknown outcomes and incomplete follow-up require explicit handling rather than being silently treated as measured non-response.

links.label: Hernan and Robins: Causal Inference: What If
CONSORT 2025: explanation and elaboration
FDA: oncology clinical-trial endpoints (2018)
OncoGuide: denominators-and-conditional-probability (pinned teaching source)

notes: “Half had a response” is incomplete until the counted group is named. The numerator counts observations meeting the event rule; the denominator identifies the relevant group or observation amount. Conditional probability P(A | B) means the probability of A among those satisfying B, with P(A | B) = P(A and B)/P(B) when P(B) is positive. It is undefined if that conditioning probability is zero. “Given” does not mean “caused by”, and the probability of a positive test among people with disease differs from the probability of disease among people with a positive test. People, lesions, blood draws and wells supply different denominators. Events per person-time are a rate, not a simple probability; repeated samples do not become independent patients. A group defined by treatment response may also be selected by underlying biology, so a conditional frequency does not show that the treatment caused the difference. A changed proportion needs its reference proportion attached, because percentages and percentage points answer different questions.

A fictional study enrols twenty people, six never receive the product, fourteen are treated, ten have evaluable scans and five meet the response rule. The observed response proportions are 5/20 = 25% among enrolled people, 5/14, about 35.7%, among treated people, and 5/10 = 50% among those with evaluable scans. The scan-evaluable group is nested within the treated group, which is nested within enrolment. Five other evaluable scans did not meet the response rule; four treated people lack evaluable scans and six were untreated, with no response outcomes supplied for those groups. Calling them confirmed nonresponders would add an assumption. A protocol may classify missing assessments as nonresponse, but that rule and its sensitivity analyses should be reported explicitly.

In a separate complete fictional cohort of 100 people, twenty recur and five of those have brain involvement. Brain involvement is 5/20 = 25% among those with recurrence and 5/100 = 5% in the original cohort. Neither is a personal forecast. In another example with forty enrolled, thirty treated, twenty evaluable and eight responses, 8/20 = 40% describes the evaluable group, whereas 8/40 = 20% describes observed responders among everyone enrolled without establishing the other outcomes. Incomplete follow-up also means recorded events divided by enrolment may not estimate risk at a chosen time; survival or competing-risk methods address defined questions under their assumptions. Safety and efficacy tables can use different analysis sets, and biomarker subgroups or later landmarks change who contributes. Multiple reports from the same participants add no independent people. Exclusion because progression prevented assessment can itself affect interpretation.

records.name: Lead time, and lead-time bias
aka: lead time in prostate cancer screening
records.tldr: Finding a cancer earlier starts the survival clock sooner, even if the date of death does not change. Counting that extra time as longer life is lead-time bias. Survival measured from diagnosis alone cannot establish that screening saves lives.
records.summary:
Lead time is the interval between the moment a screening test finds a cancer and the moment that cancer would have been diagnosed because it caused symptoms. Lead-time bias is what happens when survival is measured from diagnosis: a man whose cancer is found five years earlier appears to survive five years longer even if the date of his death is unchanged. It is why survival from diagnosis is unreliable on its own as a measure of whether a screening programme works, and why randomised screening trials report mortality in the whole invited population instead.

For prostate-specific antigen screening, estimated lead time depends on the definition and population. The following numbers are model estimates from specified settings, not a ranking of lead times across cancers. Draisma and Etzioni ran three independently built models of prostate cancer progression and detection, all calibrated to Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results incidence in United States men aged 54 to 80 between 1985 and 2000. Among screen-detected cancers that would have surfaced in the man's lifetime, mean lead time was 5.4 to 6.9 years across the three models; the original MISCAN model fitted instead to the Rotterdam section of the European screening trial gave 7.9 years. Published estimates before that work spanned 3 to 12 years. The three models agreed closely with each other for any single definition of lead time and disagreed substantially across definitions, which is the paper's real finding: the number is a property of the question, not of the disease.

The consequence is practical. Lead time is what generates overdiagnosis: if the lead time is longer than the man's remaining life, the cancer would never have troubled him, and the same modelling put overdiagnosis at 23 to 42 percent of screen-detected cancers in the United States calibration and 66 percent in the Rotterdam one. It is also why the 2018 United States task force statement expresses benefit as deaths and metastatic cases prevented per 1,000 men screened over about 13 years rather than as a survival rate, and why the two 2009 randomised trials, ERSPC and PLCO, are the evidence rather than any registry series.

GIVIO Investigators, JAMA 1994: follow-up testing
Assessment of Molecular Relapse Detection in Early-Stage Breast Cancer

notes: Why a five-year survival rate cannot settle a screening argument. Three biases push it up without anyone living longer: lead-time bias, because the clock starts earlier; length bias, because a test that samples the population at intervals preferentially catches slow-growing cancers that sit around waiting to be found; and overdiagnosis, because cancers that would never have surfaced are added to the numerator of survivors. All three run in the same direction. Mortality in a randomised invited population is immune to all three, which is why it is the endpoint the trials used.

Lead time is not the same as overdiagnosis, although the two are produced by the same mechanism. Lead time is how much earlier the diagnosis came. Overdiagnosis is the case where the lead time exceeded the rest of the man's life, so the diagnosis never needed to come at all. A long lead time with a long life left is exactly what screening is for.

Lead time is the interval between defined earlier and later detection events. Lead-time bias occurs when that timing difference is mistaken for a better outcome. In a fictional course, detection at year 4 and death at year 6 gives two years from diagnosis. Moving detection to year 3 with death still at year 6 gives three recorded years without adding life. Similarly, labelling post-treatment recurrence at a blood signal before imaging confirmation can mechanically lengthen survival measured from recurrence. Align the endpoint, qualifying event and clock origin. Ten months of detection lead time is not ten added months of life. Earlier effective intervention could help, but its benefit needs separate evidence; correcting the clock alone does not solve selection, confounding or missing follow-up.

Length bias favours conditions with longer detectable preclinical periods. Overdiagnosis means detecting disease that would not have caused clinical harm during the person's lifetime. Neither is another name for lead-time bias. Screening examples explain the distinctions but cannot establish their magnitude in post-treatment molecular monitoring.

A monitoring strategy includes its schedule, positive-result rule and resulting action. Comparing that strategy with a meaningful alternative from a common origin, such as randomisation, can assess clinical outcomes and harms. Counting all assigned participants avoids selecting only those with detectable earlier signals. Analysis must also address when groups entered, how follow-up ended, whether positive tests triggered extra imaging and whether people without prior detection were omitted. c-TRAK TN tested a specific blood-surveillance and intervention design; its detection and feasibility findings do not establish a beneficial intervention window for every early signal. A fictional contrast of median survival of 24 months after blood detection versus 18 after imaging detection, without a common-origin comparison, cannot show that testing saves lives. Some or all of the difference could arise from the earlier clock or other group differences.

The same timing distinction extends beyond the prostate-screening context of this record. Historical breast-cancer surveillance trials illustrate why strategy and outcome must stay together. Rosselli Del Turco and colleagues' 1994 trial enrolled 1,243 surgically treated patients with unilateral invasive breast cancer and no metastases. Adding six-monthly chest radiographs and bone scans detected more isolated intrathoracic and bone metastases, 112 versus 71, and the report described earlier detection of recurrences in that group; five-year relapse-free survival, which stops at detection, was significantly lower with intensive follow-up, while five-year mortality was 18.6% versus 19.5%, with no mortality improvement reported. The separate GIVIO trial enrolled 1,320 women and reported no overall-survival or quality-of-life difference, and no significant difference in time to recurrence detection. Thus the trials should not both be described as showing earlier detection: only the first reported it. Their results do not establish equivalence or the effects of modern imaging and treatment, and a nonsignificant comparison is not proof of exactly zero benefit.

In ctDNA monitoring studies, measured lead time is the date of a defined later event minus the date of the first qualifying positive blood sample, and it is conditional: a median over people with both an earlier positive and a later recurrence leaves out recurrences with no earlier positive, and people who are positive but have not yet recurred are censored. In a prospective breast-cancer study with blood taken every 3 months in the first year and every 6 months after, detection preceded clinical relapse by a median of 10.7 months (95% CI 8.1 to 19.1) in a combined cohort of 144, and brain-only relapse was detected in 1 of 6 patients (Garcia-Murillas 2019). Because draws and scans are both intermittent, the gap begins at an observed draw and cannot locate biological onset, and an earlier signal shows earlier detection and not longer survival, which is the lead-time bias problem.

State how lead time was estimated. A simple median of completed positive-to-recurrence intervals is conditional on that selected group; a time-to-event analysis can also incorporate censored follow-up. People without a prior positive and people positive without a later recurrence therefore need explicit dispositions under the study definition. They are not automatically zero-month, infinite or missing intervals interchangeable across studies.

A fictional timing problem illustrates why group entry matters: if a group is defined by a blood-positive result at month 6, its members had to remain observable until that result. Assigning their earlier follow-up to the positive group can create immortal-time bias. A prespecified landmark or a time-varying exposure analysis addresses different timing questions; the comparison must state its origin, eligibility and handling of later events. This is a study-design reading rule, not evidence that a surveillance policy improves outcomes.

records.name: Reading scientific graphs
records.tldr: Read a graph with its caption and methods: identify who was measured, what changed, the outcome, the comparison and the uncertainty. A visible pattern does not supply those missing details.
records.summary: A scientific graph needs its caption and methods to identify the population, independent measurement unit, intervention, outcome, comparison and uncertainty. Axis scale, baseline and time origin can change what a visible difference means. Biological units and repeated technical measurements must remain distinct, and different error bars describe different quantities. A plotted association, growth reduction or late survival plateau requires its own interpretation before any claim about causality or patient benefit.

links.label: SuperPlots: Communicating reproducibility and variability in cell biology.
NIST: graphical techniques
CONSORT 2025: reporting randomized trials
OncoGuide: reading-a-graph-in-five-passes (pinned teaching source)

notes: Read a graph as an answer to a question before interpreting its shape. Establish who or what contributes independent observations, what intervention was given and when, which outcome and units the axes show, what baseline or control supplies the comparison, and what uncertainty or missing information remains. Entry criteria, dose, measurement site, time origin and follow-up can change the answer. A whole product and one component are different interventions; cell activity, tumour size, recurrence and survival are different outcomes. A mouse-volume graph cannot become a patient-survival result because the plotted separation is large. This five-pass reading habit is a teaching synthesis, not a score certifying a study; an explicitly unreported independent sample count remains useful information.

Biological replicates are independent units relevant to the question, such as donors or animals. Technical repeats measure the same material again: three tubes or ten wells from one donor still represent one donor. Twelve measurements from three donors therefore require an analysis that accounts for repeated measurements, rather than treating all twelve as independent people. Error bars must be defined. Standard deviation describes observation variability, standard error concerns precision of an estimated mean, and a confidence interval follows a specified procedure and assumptions. On logarithmic axes equal distances represent equal ratios; on linear axes they represent equal differences. A truncated axis may emphasise a small difference, so read the numbers as well as the shape. Missing observations are not measured zeros, and a complete caption does not substitute for sound methods.

In a fictional animal experiment, four independent animals contribute to each group. Both groups start with average tumour volume 100 cubic millimetres; at day 28, control averages 1,000 and treated 300. The treated average is 70% below control but three times its starting size: reduced growth relative to control, rather than shrinkage below baseline. Twenty wells from one animal would still represent one independent animal. For a Kaplan-Meier curve, the same reading habit requires event definition, starting clock, censoring and numbers still at risk. A flat late tail based on few observations cannot support a precise late estimate simply because it looks stable.

records.name: Population versus individual risk
records.tldr: A group event frequency does not determine one person's future. A personal probability estimate needs a suitable model, relevant inputs and evaluation in the setting where it will be used.
records.summary: An observed group frequency describes a specified outcome, population, treatment context and time horizon. A probability estimate for an individual adds a prediction model and relevant inputs, with uncertainty. Ranking people well does not establish accurate probabilities, and performance in one hospital, subgroup or treatment era does not establish performance elsewhere. A model predicting outcomes under existing care also does not automatically estimate the benefit of changing that care.

links.label: NCI: understanding cancer prognosis
TRIPOD-Cluster: model evaluation across settings
Hernan and Robins: Causal Inference: What If
OncoGuide: population-vs-individual-risk (pinned teaching source)
Collins et al.: TRIPOD+AI prediction-model reporting guidance (2024)
ICH E9(R1): estimands, intercurrent events and sensitivity analysis (May 2021)

notes: Population risk describes a defined group's outcomes, such as first recurrence by five years after surgery among people receiving specified care. An individual prediction applies a model and assumptions to one person's characteristics. Neither precise printing nor more biomarkers establishes that the estimate fits the situation. The model may omit relevant biology, use imperfect measurements or reflect another treatment era. Calibration asks whether groups assigned similar probabilities experience approximately the corresponding outcome frequencies; discrimination asks whether the model ranks outcomes well. Good ranking does not ensure accurate probabilities. Evaluation outside the development data is important, but performance can still vary by hospital, treatment context or subgroup. Model name and version, required inputs, missing-value rules, population, treatment, endpoint and horizon determine what the probability means, with uncertainty around performance measures.

In a fictional fully followed cohort of 100 people, twenty events by five years give a group proportion of 20%. That does not mean each person experiences one fifth of an event or identify who will have it. Suppose a model assigns 10% risk to a particular profile. About ten events among 100 comparable people in an informative independent evaluation would support calibration near that prediction, without certifying every subgroup or a different treatment sequence. Multiplying the cohort's 20% by a published marker hazard ratio and a treatment hazard ratio does not produce a validated personal probability. The ratios may come from different populations, adjusted models, endpoints and clocks, and a hazard ratio is not a fixed-time risk ratio. These examples are invented and supply no personal prognosis.

A model that ranks outcomes well at Hospital A may need evaluation at Hospital B before its printed probabilities can be trusted there, particularly if treatment and follow-up differ. Relevant calibration, outcome definitions, horizon, inputs and uncertainty matter. A post-treatment test cannot simply replace a model's required pretreatment input, or vice versa. Risk under current care is also different from benefit from changing care: outcome prediction alone does not estimate a treatment effect. An uncertain but appropriately evaluated estimate can help a discussion without promising an outcome. A confidence interval for a group parameter is not a range of individual futures, and a narrow subgroup may contain too little information for precise personalisation.

Before using a calculator, record its exact name, version and recalibration; required input definitions, units, specimen dates and missing-value rules; development population, care era and received treatments; and predicted endpoint, origin and horizon. Ask how independent evaluation checked discrimination, calibration, selected cutpoints and uncertainty in the intended setting. TRIPOD+AI covers reporting of regression and machine-learning prediction studies; it is not a quality appraisal tool or proof that acting on a score helps. If a fictional calculator requires a residual postoperative marker but only a pretreatment result exists, do not substitute it or invent a correction with unrelated hazard ratios. An unknown input is not negative, and a printed 85% remains a model estimate rather than a guarantee.

In a fictional study, a negative blood test is associated with favourable five-year outcomes while everyone receives standard treatment. Those data do not establish that stopping treatment after a negative result is safe. The missing question compares the proposed result-guided strategy with the relevant alternative, with matched sampling time, population, event, uncertainty and follow-up. Pretreatment, on-treatment and surgical samples describe different states. A later landmark includes only people eligible at that time and excludes earlier events; the last sample available during year one is not automatically an early postoperative sample. Analytical reliability, prognosis, treatment-effect prediction and benefit from a test-guided action require distinct evidence.

records.name: Cross-trial comparison
records.tldr: Results from separate studies can differ because the people, care or measurements differ. Comparing their headline percentages does not by itself show which treatment works better.
records.summary: A comparison between separate studies must account for differences in participants, treatment, background care, endpoints, clocks and follow-up. Randomisation protects the comparison within a trial; it does not randomise participants between unrelated trials. Formal indirect comparisons can retain within-trial contrasts through a common comparator, but depend on compatible effect modifiers and methods. A higher headline percentage in one study is insufficient to rank treatments.

links.label: The results of direct and indirect treatment comparisons in meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
Cochrane: network comparisons and transitivity
FDA: oncology clinical-trial endpoints (2018)
OncoGuide: cross-trial-comparison (pinned teaching source)

notes: A higher percentage in one paper is a reason to examine its study, rather than proof that its treatment is better. Randomisation protects comparisons within a trial, not between separately conducted trials. Comparing their experimental arms discards that protection. Disease burden, biomarker assay and threshold, prior treatment, background care, dose, endpoint rules, analysis population and follow-up can differ. Formal indirect comparison through a common comparator preserves each trial's treatment-versus-control contrast but still requires compatible questions and methods. Pooling active arms across trials is prone to bias, and even an adjusted indirect estimate remains less secure than a suitable direct comparison (Bucher and colleagues, 1997). Network meta-analysis adds a transitivity assumption: important effect modifiers must be sufficiently comparable across the network. A shared drug name or statistical agreement cannot establish that unmeasured compatibility. Similar endpoint labels can hide different definitions: a clinical benefit rate may include different durations of stable disease. Adjustment for measured differences does not remove every bias, and lower hazard ratios against different comparators cannot automatically rank treatments.

Two fictional single-arm studies each enrol 100 people with the same response definition, assessment period and complete denominator. In the favourable baseline group, A has 40 responses among 80 people (50%) and B has 12 among 20 (60%). In the other group, A has 4/20 (20%) and B 24/80 (30%). Overall, A has 44% response and B 36%, despite B's higher rate in both groups. A enrolled an 80/20 mixture of the two groups, while B enrolled 20/80. Composition reverses the headline ranking. This arithmetic does not establish that B is superior: people were not randomised between studies, and one measured feature cannot resolve every difference.

A fictional vaccine report of 90% recurrence-free at two years in selected postoperative patients cannot be ranked against 30% objective response in a different advanced-disease drug study. Immune response, pathological response, imaging response and survival are different outcomes in different settings. A comparative effect estimate needs a shared clinical question and defensible design. For time-to-event results, align the event definition, origin, assessment schedule, cutoff and follow-up as well as population and care. FDA's December 2018 endpoint guidance warns that external survival comparisons can reflect selection, imaging and supportive-care differences. Neither fictional example certifies an actual indirect comparison.

records.name: Confidence interval
records.tldr: A confidence interval shows an estimate's precision under a stated method. A 95% method covers the fixed true value in about 95% of repeated valid applications; it does not assign a 95% probability to the value lying in this particular interval.
records.summary: Because a trial studies a sample rather than every patient in the world, its estimate carries uncertainty, and the confidence interval expresses it: more information often narrows the interval, while the method, data structure and assumptions also matter. For a conventional matching two-sided 95% interval and test, a hazard-ratio interval that excludes 1.0 corresponds to a p-value below 0.05; for a difference in months or percentage points, the interval must exclude zero. Reading the interval rather than just the point estimate shows how large or small the true benefit could plausibly be, and limits close to no effect should be read with the whole interval, clinical question and assumptions. Their position alone does not quantify how the result would change under different data or analyses.

links.label: NIST: confidence limits and repeated coverage
Statistical tests, P values, confidence intervals, and power: a guide to misinterpretations.
Greenland et al., 2016: statistical tests and confidence-interval interpretation
OncoGuide: confidence-interval (pinned teaching source)

notes: A frequentist confidence interval describes estimation precision using a procedure with a stated coverage rate under its assumptions. Across repeated valid applications, a 95% procedure would include the fixed true parameter in 95% of its intervals. This does not assign a 95% probability to that parameter being inside one interval after it has been calculated, or describe a range containing 95% of patients. The result depends on the data structure, estimator, confidence level, model and calculation method, including adjustment, missing-data handling and multiplicity. More observations often improve precision but do not remove biased measurement, confounding or a wrong model.

The no-difference value is zero for differences and one for ratios. Including it does not prove equality. A fictional hazard ratio of 0.70 with an interval of 0.35 to 1.40 leaves substantial benefit and harm compatible with the analysis; 0.70 with an interval of 0.65 to 0.76 is more precise. Neither establishes personal benefit or applicability to another population. Likewise, a risk-difference interval of -8 to +10 percentage points does not establish equivalence. That requires justified, preferably prespecified lower and upper bounds and a suitable equivalence analysis; non-inferiority asks a separate question about one permitted-loss margin. Compare groups by estimating their difference directly, rather than judging whether two separate intervals overlap. Many unadjusted intervals also raise a multiplicity problem.

For a fictional binary outcome in 50 of 100 independent people, the normal-approximation standard error is sqrt(0.50 × 0.50/100) = 0.05. The approximate 95% interval is 0.50 ± 1.96 × 0.05, or 40.2% to 59.8%. With 5,000 of 10,000 people, the proportion stays 50% but the standard error becomes 0.005 and the interval 49.02% to 50.98%. Small counts, proportions near zero or one, clustering and incomplete outcomes may require other methods. A hand-picked set of ten such intervals, nine containing a fixed 50% truth and one missing it, illustrates coverage but does not measure a procedure's coverage rate. A 95% method need not cover in exactly 95% of a small set. Narrower bounds indicate greater sampling precision, not less bias.

A prediction interval addresses a future observation and includes additional variability. A Bayesian credible interval gives a probability interpretation conditional on the chosen model and prior. These are different constructions, not alternative names for a frequentist confidence interval.

records.name: Preclinical
records.tldr: Evidence from laboratory, animal and computational work used to study mechanisms, activity and safety. It can guide human studies without establishing patient benefit.
records.summary: Preclinical and nonclinical work studies mechanisms, activity, exposure and safety using specified models. Such experiments can occur before or alongside human studies. Evidence that a model responds does not establish a useful treatment for patients. FDA nonclinical requirements depend on the product and context; its published approaches include justified reductions or replacements of animal studies, so a universal two-species requirement is inaccurate.

links.label: Wikipedia
Studying cancer immunotherapy using patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) in humanized mice
What exactly is 'N' in cell culture and animal experiments?
The ARRIVE guidelines 2.0: Updated guidelines for reporting animal research.
FDA: purpose and safety context of preclinical research
FDA: context-specific nonclinical studies and new approach methodologies
Reporting animal research: Explanation and elaboration for the ARRIVE guidelines 2.0.

notes: In-vitro, in-vivo and human-derived describe experimental setting or origin, not validation of treatment in patients. A cell line can test a direct cell effect, while an immune-intact mouse can test selected tissue and immune interactions; neither reproduces every human cancer, prior treatment or physiology. An immune mechanism needs its relevant components represented and functional. Human tissue grown in a dish or grafted into a mouse remains model evidence about that intervention.

Name the intervention, control, outcome and units before counting replication. The biological unit is the entity about which conclusions are sought, such as a donor. The experimental unit receives an independently assigned intervention; the observational unit is measured. A cage assigned together or a preparation treated before being split can make the animals or wells subsamples. More measured cells do not become more assigned mice. Biological and technical replicate labels vary, so inspect sampling, preparation, allocation and measurement. Repeating runs tests consistency without adding donor identities. Analysing correlated subsamples as independent replicates is pseudoreplication.

Fictional design: each of two donors supplies six wells, three control and three treated. The twelve distinct wells receive independent randomized assignments within donor, separate treatment and no mutual influence, while the analysis retains donor nesting. There are twelve assigned wells and two donor sources, not twelve donors. No cell counts or recommended sample size are supplied. If instead a donor preparation is treated before being split, its wells are subsamples of that assignment. Adding cells does not add wells or donors. This distinction follows from the stipulated allocation, not from a universal rule that wells always are independent.

A controlled fictional mouse study in which local treatment changes a distant tumour can support a distant effect in that model. If a controlled immune-cell depletion reduces that effect, it supports a contribution under those tested conditions. Further steps include safely achievable human exposure, relevant target biology, safety and comparative patient outcomes. Mouse tumour volume is not patient survival, and a laboratory effect size or universal model threshold does not establish clinical benefit. A reproducible mechanism can coexist with an impractical or harmful clinical exposure. These are limits on the inference, not a guarantee that any particular model result will translate.

Retain the model or specimen, treatment and comparator, assigned units and subsamples, exclusions, allocation, blinded assessment, timing, dose, readout units and uncertainty. A cell count, cubic-millimetre tumour volume and named assay signal are different measurements. ARRIVE supports appraisal of animal-study reporting rather than proving a conclusion. Exploratory academic experiments and regulatory safety studies have different purposes and requirements. FDA's context-specific nonclinical approaches, including new approach methodologies, do not validate every model for personal treatment selection.

records.name: Calibration: reliability diagrams and the Brier score
records.tldr: Calibration checks whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies for the same population, outcome and time horizon. Correct ranking or a correct overall average is insufficient.
records.summary: Calibration compares predicted probabilities with observed outcome frequencies in a defined population and time horizon. A model can rank people well while overstating their risks. Calibration curves and suitable summaries assess agreement with uncertainty. The Brier score averages squared differences between predicted probabilities and individual binary outcomes; it assesses overall prediction error rather than calibration alone. Incomplete follow-up and competing events need methods matched to the predicted outcome.

links.label: Wikipedia: Brier score
Graf et al., Assessment and comparison of prognostic classification schemes for survival data (Statistics in Medicine 1999)
Wikipedia
Calibration: the Achilles heel of predictive analytics.
Evaluation of clinical prediction models (part 2): how to undertake an external validation study.

notes: Compare predicted and observed frequencies across risk groups or a flexible calibration curve, with finite-sample uncertainty. Calibration-in-the-large compares the average prediction with the overall outcome rate. Under the named calibration model, slope below 1 suggests predictions that are too extreme and above 1 insufficient spread; intercept near 0 and slope near 1 still do not guarantee agreement everywhere on a flexible curve. A constant prediction can match average risk without ranking anyone. Conversely, high discrimination does not establish probability accuracy.

Two fictional 100-person groups have complete five-year outcomes. Predicting 20 and 40 per cent when 10 and 30 events occur preserves their group order but predicts 60 events instead of 40. In a second independent example, predictions of 10 and 50 per cent with 20 and 40 events give 60 predicted and 60 observed overall, or 30 per cent of 200, while both group predictions remain wrong. These invented comparisons illustrate distinct failures; they do not forecast a particular patient's outcome.

Retain predictions stored before outcomes, model and assay versions, endpoint, target population, treatment era and horizon. Compare frequencies at the same time using a calibration curve or named summary and uncertainty. Treating people censored before the horizon as event-free can mislead; account for incomplete follow-up and relevant competing events. Changed eligibility, care or baseline outcome frequency can change calibration, and an updated model needs evaluation. Checking only an overall average or displaying a narrow numerical range establishes little about model or input uncertainty. Calibration neither identifies which individual will have an event nor establishes benefit from acting on the model.
